## Morelia — a touch of Spain in Mexico!

Morelia is one of the country's most beautiful yet lesser-known cities. It is the capital of Michoacán state, but much about it feels distinctly un-Mexican. In many ways it resembles an old Spanish town that has retained its colonial character. Walking along its streets and squares, past churches and monasteries, you may feel as though you are in a small town in Spain. The city was originally called Valladolid; only in 1828 was it renamed in honour of independence hero José María Morelos.

In 1991, the city was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in recognition of its well-preserved colonial architecture and the layout of its historic centre.

## Morelia — Mexico's Pink City!

All of Morelia's main attractions are in its historic centre. Morelia Cathedral is considered one of the most beautiful in Mexico. The Sanctuary of Our Lady of Guadalupe (Santuario de Guadalupe) stands on the edge of the historic centre. One of Mexico's most beautiful churches, it contains a series of 17th-century paintings depicting the 'victory' of Spanish missionaries over the 'barbarian' religious traditions of the Aztecs. The buildings reflect architectural styles that dominated Mexico in different periods, yet almost all are made of pink cantera stone, giving the old city a harmonious appearance. That is why Morelia is so often called 'Ciudad Rosa' (the Pink City).

Visitors ascend to Morro da Urca from Praia Vermelha and can then continue towards Sugarloaf Mountain. This stop deserves time in its own right: water, yachts, green hillsides and dense urban neighbourhoods open up before you.

From the viewpoints, you can see Guanabara Bay, Botafogo Bay and the neighbourhoods of southern Rio. Stopping between the ascents offers the chance to see the panorama from different elevations. Walkers also have the option of a separate hiking trail on Morro da Urca, which can be chosen as an activity in its own right.

On a cable-car excursion, Morro da Urca is a destination in its own right rather than merely a transfer point. The visit depends on the available time, weather and chosen itinerary.

Morro de São Paulo is located on Tinharé Island off the coast of Bahia. The catamaran journey from Salvador takes about an hour, making the island an easy addition to a longer itinerary through the state.

First, Second, Third and Fourth Beaches have different atmospheres. Closer to the village, there are more hotels, restaurants and nightlife, while Fourth Beach is better suited to a quieter stay.

Alongside the ocean, Morro de São Paulo has a historic quarter and a lighthouse with a viewpoint. This combination makes it possible to mix several days of relaxation with walks, activities on the water and short trips around the island.

Mosquera looks like a pale strip of sand in the middle of the ocean. This low-lying islet lies between Baltra and North Seymour. There is little vegetation, but plenty of sea lions. Along the water's edge, they return from swimming, rest beside one another and call back and forth. Watching their everyday life becomes the main attraction of a landing here.

It is a pleasure to walk slowly along the sandy shore. Red crabs appear among the dark rocks, while coastal birds fly overhead. You may encounter the lava gull, a rare Galápagos bird. A single animal or bird can easily hold your attention, and this little island proves far more interesting than it looks from the deck of a yacht.

Mosquera is ideal for travellers who want to spend time beside the sea observing animal behaviour. Its sandy coast offers open views and good light for photography. Leave the sea lions a clear path to the water, and watch how their movements change as they pass from land into the ocean.

Mount Roraima is one of the most recognisable tabletop mountains of the Guiana Highlands. Its flat summit rises above the savannah on sheer rock walls, and clouds often conceal parts of its cliffs. From below, the mountain looks like a world apart from the open plains surrounding it.

The walking route to the plateau crosses savannah, rivers and an ascent to the base of the cliffs. At the top, travellers encounter rocky surfaces, unusual stone formations and shifting mist. A multi-day journey on Roraima reveals a succession of landscapes, from the plains to the high mountain plateau.
